rewritten_text:
Mrs. Clay's feelings had proved stronger than her ambition. For the young man's sake, she had given up her chance to keep trying to win Sir Walter. But she has cleverness as well as feelings, and it remains uncertain whose schemes will succeed in the end. After preventing her from becoming Sir Walter's wife, he may yet be coaxed and flattered into making her the wife of Sir William.

Sir Walter and Elizabeth were undoubtedly shocked and humiliated by the loss of their companion and the discovery that they had misjudged her. They could, of course, turn to their distinguished cousins for comfort. But they would long feel that there is only half as much pleasure in flattering and following other people when nobody flatters and follows you in return.

Anne soon felt sure that Lady Russell intended to give Captain Wentworth the affection he deserved. Only one thing disturbed her happiness about the future: she had no relatives to offer him whom a sensible man could admire. In that respect, she felt her disadvantage painfully. The difference in their wealth meant nothing to her and never caused her a moment's regret. But she had no family who would welcome him and value him properly. She could offer no family respectability, harmony, or kindness to match the goodness and immediate welcome she found among his brothers and sisters. This caused her as much pain as she could feel while being otherwise so deeply happy. There were only two friends in the world she could add to his circle: Lady Russell and Mrs. Smith. He was, however, quite ready to become attached to both. Despite all Lady Russell's past mistakes, he could now sincerely appreciate her. As long as he was not required to say she had been right to separate them originally, he was willing to say almost anything else in her favor. Mrs. Smith, meanwhile, had several reasons for quickly and permanently winning his friendship.

The kindness she had recently shown Anne was enough by itself. Their marriage gave her two friends instead of taking one away. She was their first visitor once they had settled into married life. Captain Wentworth helped her recover her husband's property in the West Indies, writing letters and acting on her behalf. He guided her through every small difficulty in the case with all the energy of a fearless man and a friend determined to help. In doing so, he fully repaid all the help she had given his wife, or had ever intended to give her.

He made no further attempt. The boys lay counting the slow moments until it seemed time itself must have ended and eternity begun to grow old; at last they gratefully observed that the sun was going down.

One of the snores stopped. Injun Joe raised himself, glanced about, and smiled sourly at his companion, whose head had sunk upon his knees. Prodding him with a foot, he said:

“Here! A fine watchman you are! Still, it's all right—nothing's happened.”

“Lord! Was I asleep?”

“Oh, a little, a little. Almost time to move along, pard. What shall we do with the bit of swag we've still got?”

“Don't know—leave it here, same as always, I suppose. No point carrying it off before we head south. Six hundred and fifty in silver makes a load.”

“Well, all right. Another trip here won't hurt.”

“No; only I'd come after dark, the way we used to. That's better.”

“Yes, but listen: I may have to wait a good while for the right chance at that business. Something might happen; this ain't such a safe place. We'll bury it properly, and good and deep.”

“That's a good notion,” said his comrade. He crossed the room, knelt, lifted a hearth-stone towards the back, and brought out a bag with a pleasant jingle. Taking twenty or thirty dollars for himself and the same amount for Injun Joe, he handed the bag to Joe, who was already kneeling in a corner and digging with his bowie-knife.

In an instant the boys forgot every fear and misery. Their eager eyes followed each movement. Such luck! Its magnificence was beyond anything they could imagine. Six hundred dollars would make six boys rich! Here was treasure-hunting under the most fortunate conditions: there would be no troublesome guessing about where to dig. They kept nudging one another, expressive nudges whose meaning was perfectly clear: “Well, aren't you glad we're here now!”

Joe's knife hit something.

“Hello!” he said.

“What've you found?” asked his companion.

“A rotten bit of plank—no, I reckon it's a box. Here, lend a hand and we'll find out why it's here. Never mind; I've knocked a hole through.”

He thrust his hand inside and pulled it out again—

“Man, it's money!”

Both men inspected the handful of coins. They were gold. The boys overhead felt just as excited and delighted as the men.

Joe's companion said:

“We can get this done quick. There's an old rusty pick lying in the weeds in that corner across the fireplace. I spotted it a minute back.”

At last, “Charles Evrémonde, known as Darnay,” was brought forward to face the charge.

His judges sat on the bench wearing feathered hats. Almost everyone else wore a rough red cap with a three-colored badge. Looking at the jury and the unruly crowd, he might have thought the normal order reversed: criminals seemed to be putting honest men on trial. The city's lowest and cruelest people controlled the scene, in a city that had never lacked such people. Unrestrained, they loudly commented, applauded, protested, guessed at the outcome, and tried to hasten it. Most of the men carried some kind of weapon. Among the women, some had knives or daggers, some ate and drank as they watched, and many knitted. One of those knitting kept a spare piece of work under her arm. She sat in the front row beside a man Darnay had not seen since arriving at the Barrier, but whom he immediately recognized as Defarge. Once or twice she whispered in the man's ear, and Darnay thought she must be his wife. What struck him most, however, was that although the pair sat as close to him as possible, neither looked his way. They seemed to be waiting stubbornly for something, watching the jury and nothing else. Beneath the President sat Doctor Manette in his usual plain clothes. As far as the prisoner could see, the Doctor and Mr. Lorry were the only men outside the court officials who wore their normal clothing instead of the rough revolutionary dress of the Carmagnole.

The public prosecutor accused Charles Evrémonde, known as Darnay, of being an emigrant. Under the decree banishing all emigrants on pain of death, his life was owed to the Republic. It did not matter that this decree had been issued after his return to France. He was there, and the decree existed. He had been arrested in France, and they demanded his head.

“Cut off his head!” the crowd shouted. “An enemy of the Republic!”

The President rang his bell to quiet them, then asked the prisoner whether it was true that he had lived in England for many years.

It certainly was.

Then wasn't he an emigrant? What did he call himself?

He hoped he was not an emigrant in the sense intended by the law.

Why not? the President asked.

Because he had willingly given up a title and a social position he disliked, and had left his country before, he pointed out, the court's current meaning of “emigrant” had come into use. He had gone to England to earn his own living, rather than live on the work of France's already overburdened people.
